clinicalPearls: Rabies is a rapidly progressive acute CNS infection by rabies virus (a lyssavirus, family Rhabdoviridae), normally transmitted via the bite of an infected animal; it has encephalitic and paralytic forms that progress to death (p.1650).

Worldwide, ~99% of human rabies is transmitted from dogs in countries with endemic canine rabies; endemic canine rabies causes an estimated 59,000 human deaths annually, with most deaths in Asia and Africa and rural populations and children disproportionately affected (p.1650-1651).
Incubation period is usually 20-90 days but in rare cases may be as short as a few days or longer than 1 year (p.1651).

Earliest specific neurologic symptoms are paresthesias, pain, or pruritus near the exposure site, occurring in 50-80% of patients and strongly suggesting rabies; the wound has usually healed by this point (p.1652).
Two acute neurologic forms occur: encephalitic (furious) in ~80% and paralytic (dumb) in ~20% (p.1652).

Encephalitic rabies presents as atypical encephalitis with relative preservation of consciousness; episodes of hyperexcitability alternate with periods of complete lucidity that shorten as disease progresses (p.1652).

Early brainstem involvement produces the classic hydrophobia (involuntary painful contraction of diaphragm and accessory respiratory, laryngeal, and pharyngeal muscles on swallowing liquids) and aerophobia (same response to a draft of air) (p.1652).

Autonomic dysfunction is common and may cause hypersalivation, gooseflesh, cardiac arrhythmia, and priapism; hypersalivation plus pharyngeal dysfunction produces the classic 'foaming at the mouth' (p.1652).

Paralytic rabies features early prominent flaccid weakness often beginning in the bitten extremity, progressing to quadriparesis and facial weakness, with sphincter involvement common and sensory involvement usually mild (p.1652).

The Negri body (eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion in brain neurons, e.g. cerebellar Purkinje cells and hippocampal pyramidal neurons) is the most characteristic pathologic finding, but is NOT seen in all cases (p.1651-1652).

Diagnosis should be considered in patients with acute atypical encephalitis or acute flaccid paralysis, including those in whom Guillain-Barre syndrome is suspected; absence of an animal-bite history is common in North America due to unrecognized bat exposures (p.1653).
Postexposure prophylaxis must be initiated after a recognized exposure and before any symptoms or signs develop; the emphasis for prevention is on PEP (p.1652).
harrison.pathophysiology: Rabies virus, a single-strand negative-sense RNA lyssavirus (family Rhabdoviridae), is usually inoculated by an animal bite. During most of the incubation period the virus remains at or near the inoculation site; in muscle it binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junctions. It spreads centripetally along peripheral nerves toward the spinal cord or brainstem by retrograde fast axonal transport (up to ~250 mm/d, with ~12-h delays at each synapse). Once in the CNS it disseminates rapidly along neuroanatomic connections; neurons are prominently infected while astrocyte infection is unusual. After CNS infection is established there is centrifugal spread along sensory and autonomic nerves to salivary glands, heart, adrenal glands, and skin; viral replication in salivary gland acinar cells leads to secretion in saliva (the vehicle of animal transmission). There is no well-documented evidence for hematogenous spread. CNS inflammatory changes are mild (mononuclear infiltrate, perivascular cuffing, microglial Babes nodules) with little neuronal death; clinical disease is attributed to neuronal dysfunction rather than death, with oxidative stress from mitochondrial dysfunction implicated. (p.1650-1652)
additionalDifferentials: Anti-NMDA receptor and other autoimmune encephalitides
Postinfectious (immune-mediated) encephalomyelitis (following influenza, measles, mumps, or neural-tissue rabies vaccine)
Rabies hysteria / somatic symptom disorder (psychological response to fear of rabies)
Misdiagnosis as a primary psychiatric disorder
infectionMimics: Postinfectious encephalomyelitis after influenza, measles, or mumps
nonInfectiousMimics: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (especially young females; behavioral changes, autonomic instability, hypoventilation, seizures)
Rabies hysteria (somatic symptom disorder) with shorter course and eventual recovery
additionalInvestigations: Rabies virus-specific serum neutralizing antibodies (diagnostic in a previously unimmunized patient; may not develop until late and some patients die without them)
Rabies virus-specific neutralizing antibodies in CSF (suggest rabies encephalitis regardless of immunization status)
RT-PCR for rabies virus RNA (highly sensitive/specific; saliva, skin biopsy, CSF [less sensitive], brain tissue; genetic sequencing can identify the variant/source)
Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing for rabies virus antigen (skin biopsy and brain tissue; in skin, antigen detected in cutaneous nerves at the base of hair follicles)
Skin biopsy from hairy skin at the nape of the neck
CSF examination (typically mild mononuclear pleocytosis with mildly elevated protein)
MRI brain (variable, nonspecific brainstem/gray-matter signal abnormalities); CT usually normal; EEG nonspecific
redFlags: Near-100% fatal once symptomatic, so post-exposure prophylaxis is everything - do NOT delay PEP after a recognized exposure.
Paresthesias, pain, or pruritus at a healed animal-bite site preceding neurologic illness strongly suggest rabies.
Hydrophobia or aerophobia with preserved consciousness (atypical encephalitis) is essentially diagnostic of encephalitic rabies.

Absence of a recalled animal bite does NOT exclude rabies - bat exposures are frequently unrecognized; consider PEP when a small child or sleeping adult shared a space with a bat and an unrecognized bite cannot be reliably excluded.
Negative antemortem rabies-specific laboratory tests never exclude the diagnosis; repeat testing may be needed.
Acute flaccid paralysis resembling Guillain-Barre syndrome may be paralytic rabies - fever, bladder dysfunction, normal sensory exam, and CSF pleocytosis favor rabies.
harrison.prognosis: Rabies is an almost uniformly fatal disease but is nearly always preventable after recognized exposures with appropriate postexposure therapy during the early incubation period. Most patients die within several days of symptom onset despite aggressive critical-care support. There is no established treatment and no antiviral has demonstrated efficacy; aggressive supportive care has yielded at least 33 documented survivors (many recently reported from India), but recent treatment failures (>60) have far outnumbered successes. All but 2 of the 33 documented survivors had received one or more doses of rabies vaccine before disease onset, and the unvaccinated survivors had neutralizing antibodies in CSF at presentation. A palliative approach may be appropriate for patients who are not candidates for aggressive management. (p.1654)
pitfalls: Rabies is often not considered until late in the clinical course in North America even with a typical presentation.
Relying on a history of animal bite to make the diagnosis - many cases (especially bat-associated) have no recalled exposure.
Assuming absence of hydrophobia excludes rabies - lack of hydrophobia is not unusual.
Misdiagnosing paralytic rabies as Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Treating negative antemortem rabies-specific tests as exclusionary.
Severe CSF pleocytosis (>1000 white cells/uL) is unusual for rabies and should prompt a search for an alternative diagnosis.
Delaying local wound care while awaiting the 10-day animal observation period - wound care should not be delayed.

Administering passive immunization (RIG) more than 7 days after the first vaccine dose, when endogenous antibody production has begun and passive immunization may be counterproductive; rabies vaccine and RIG must never be given at the same site.
Minor deviations from current PEP recommendations can lead to prophylaxis failure.
harrison.severityClassification: Clinical stages: incubation period (20-90 days, asymptomatic); prodrome (2-10 days: fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting; paresthesias/pain/pruritus at the wound site); acute neurologic disease - encephalitic form (~80%, 2-7 days: anxiety, agitation, hyperactivity, bizarre behavior, hallucinations, autonomic dysfunction, hydrophobia) or paralytic form (~20%, 2-10 days: flaccid limb paralysis progressing to quadriparesis with facial paralysis); then coma and death (0-14 days; recovery rare). (p.1653)
management: Immediate thorough wound cleansing and copious irrigation after any potential exposure, as the cornerstone of preventing established infection
Post-exposure prophylaxis in the unimmunised with infiltration of rabies immunoglobulin around the wound plus a course of rabies vaccine, given as early as possible during incubation
Pre-exposure rabies vaccination for high-risk groups such as veterinary and laboratory workers and travellers to endemic regions
Once symptomatic, aggressive critical-care support with sedation and control of hydrophobic and aerophobic spasms and autonomic instability, recognising the disease is almost uniformly fatal
Compassionate palliative care with symptom control where survival cannot be achieved
Barrier precautions for staff and carers, with post-exposure prophylaxis offered to those with wound or mucosal contact with the patient's secretions
Notification to public health authorities and coordination of animal-bite investigation and rabies control
